name: Negligence Test
latex: \text{Liability for Negligence} = \text{Foreseeability of Harm} \land \text{Preventability of Harm} \land \text{Failure to Take Reasonable Steps}

symbols.meaning: Whether a diligens paterfamilias (reasonable person) would foresee the reasonable possibility of conduct causing harm.
Whether a reasonable person would take reasonable steps to guard against such harm.
Whether the defendant failed to take such steps.

computes: Negligence in the South African law of delict, establishing the fault element for damages claims.
why_form:
> [!tip] Judicial Origin
> Established in *Kruger v Coetzee* 1966 (2) SA 428 (A). It splits negligence into three distinct, cumulative elements that must be proved by the plaintiff on a balance of probabilities.

> [!example] Worked Legal Application
> **Facts:** Defendant drives through a red traffic light at an intersection and collides with Plaintiff.
> 1. **Foreseeability:** A reasonable driver would foresee that driving through a red light could cause a collision and harm to others.
> 2. **Preventability:** A reasonable driver would prevent this by stopping at the red light.
> 3. **Failure:** The defendant failed to stop.
> **Conclusion:** The defendant was negligent.

name: Mandament van Spolie Requirements

symbols.meaning: The applicant was in peaceful and undisturbed possession of the property (factual possession, not necessarily legal right).
The respondent deprived the applicant of possession unlawfully (without consent or legal process).

computes: Entitlement to a mandament van spolie (restoration order), which is a possessory remedy aimed at restoring the status quo ante.
why_form:
> [!tip] Legal Rationale
> The mandament van spolie is a robust remedy designed to prevent self-help. The court does not look at the merits of who has the legal right to possess, only whether factual possession was unlawfully disrupted.

> [!example] Worked Legal Application
> **Facts:** Landlord locks Tenant out of a flat without a court order because rent is in arrears.
> 1. **Possession:** Tenant lived in the flat and had keys (factual possession).
> 2. **Deprivation:** Landlord changed the locks without consent or court order.
> **Conclusion:** Tenant is entitled to a mandament van spolie restoring possession immediately.

name: Urgent Application Test
latex: \text{Urgency relief} = \text{Explicit Urgency Circumstances} \land \text{Absence of Substantial Redress in Due Course}

symbols.meaning: Explicit details showing why the matter is urgent and cannot wait.
Explicit reasons why the applicant will not obtain substantial redress at a hearing in due course.

computes: Whether a matter qualifies to be heard as an urgent application in the Motion Court, bypassing standard time frames.
why_form:
> [!tip] Rationale
> High Court Rule 6(12) requires both elements to be set out under oath in the founding affidavit. A failure to prove either will result in the matter being struck from the roll with costs.

> [!example] Worked Legal Application
> **Facts:** Applicant seeks an interdict to stop a developer from demolishing a heritage building tomorrow.
> 1. **Circumstances:** Demolition is scheduled for tomorrow at 08:00; heritage authority has not intervened.
> 2. **No Redress:** If heard in the normal course (months away), the building will already be destroyed, making any subsequent order useless.
> **Conclusion:** Urgency established.

name: Pleadings Drafting Rules
latex: \text{Valid Pleading} = \text{Clear Statement} \land \text{Facta Probanda Only} \land \text{Plausible Cause/Defence} \land \text{Clear Prayer}

symbols.meaning: Pleadings must be clear, concise, and contain sufficient detail to enable the other side to reply.
Plead only the material facts to be proved, not the evidence (facta probantia) by which they are proved.
A statement of claim must conclude with a prayer specifying the exact relief sought.

computes: The technical and substantive validity of a pleading, shielding it from exceptions (vague and embarrassing or failing to disclose a cause of action).
why_form:
> [!tip] Pleading Rules Rationale
> Designed to define the issues in dispute clearly, prevent surprise at trial, and keep litigation structured. Non-compliance makes the pleading excipient under Rule 23.

> [!example] Worked Legal Application
> **Correct Pleading (Facta Probanda):** 'On 10 June 2026, at West Street, the defendant negligently collided with the plaintiff's vehicle.'
> **Incorrect Pleading (Facta Probantia):** 'The plaintiff will call Mr X who will testify that he saw the defendant looking at his phone before the collision.' (This is evidence, not a material fact).

name: High Court Modes of Address
filename: f- High Court Modes of Address.md

symbols.meaning: Address to a male judge directly in court.
Address to a female judge directly in court.
Third-person reference to a male judge.
Third-person reference to a female judge.

computes: Correct and respectful verbal address to a High Court, Supreme Court of Appeal, or Constitutional Court Judge.
why_form:
> [!important] Court Protocol Rule
> Never address a judge in the second person as 'you' or 'yourself'. For example: 'Could you look at Exhibit A?' is incorrect. The correct form is: 'May I ask Your Lordship to look at Exhibit A?'

> [!example] Dialogue Example
> **Counsel:** 'As Your Lordship pleases. I appear for the applicant, My Lord. If I may direct Your Lordship's attention to page 5 of the bundle...'
